core_summary: This chapter investigates covalent bonding in carbon driven by tetravalency and catenation, leading to an immense diversity of organic molecules. It examines saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons, structural isomerism, functional groups, and homologous series. The chapter details chemical properties of carbon compounds including combustion, oxidation, addition, and substitution, with focused study on ethanol and ethanoic acid, concluding with the saponification mechanism and micelle structure of soaps and detergents.
key_concepts: Covalent bonding via shared electron pairs achieving octet stability without forming ions
Versatile nature of carbon caused by catenation (self-linking) and tetravalency
Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) with single bonds versus unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes, alkynes) with double or triple bonds
Structural isomerism in compounds sharing identical molecular formulas but different structural arrangements
Functional groups (halo, alcohol, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid) imparting specific chemical characteristics
Homologous series sharing identical functional groups, formula increments of -CH2-, and mass increments of 14 u
Nomenclature rules for organic compounds following systematic IUPAC guidelines

Chemical properties: Combustion (sooty vs clean flame), Oxidation of alcohols to carboxylic acids using alkaline KMnO4 or acidified K2Cr2O7, Addition reactions (hydrogenation of vegetable oils), and Substitution reactions of alkanes with chlorine
Properties and reactions of Ethanol and Ethanoic acid (esterification, saponification, reaction with carbonates/hydrogencarbonates)
Structure and mechanism of Soap Micelles having hydrophilic ionic heads and hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails in hard vs soft water

key_terms.definition: A chemical bond formed by the equal sharing of electron pairs between two atoms.
The unique ability of carbon to form strong covalent bonds with other carbon atoms, creating long chains, branches, or rings.
The property of having four valence electrons, enabling carbon to bond with four other monovalent atoms or functional groups.
An organic compound consisting entirely of hydrogen and carbon atoms.
Phenomenon where compounds possess the same molecular formula but different structural configurations.
An atom or group of atoms attached to a hydrocarbon chain that dictates the compound's characteristic chemical properties.
A series of organic compounds having the same functional group and chemical properties, where successive members differ by a -CH2- unit.
An addition reaction adding hydrogen to unsaturated hydrocarbons in the presence of a nickel/palladium catalyst to yield saturated fats.
The reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst to form a sweet-smelling ester.
The alkaline hydrolysis of an ester or fat with sodium hydroxide to yield soap (sodium salt of fatty acid) and alcohol.
A spherical aggregate of soap molecules formed in water, with hydrophobic tails oriented inward around oil/dirt and hydrophilic heads facing outward.
An insoluble curdy precipitate formed when soap reacts with calcium and magnesium ions present in hard water.

key_takeaways: Carbon compounds have low melting/boiling points and do not conduct electricity due to covalent non-ionic bonding.
Unsaturated hydrocarbons burn with a yellow sooty flame due to incomplete combustion, whereas saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame.
Catalytic hydrogenation converts liquid unsaturated vegetable oils into solid saturated fats.
Ethanoic acid is a weak acid compared to mineral HCl because it only partially dissociates in aqueous solution.
Detergents overcome hard water soap limitations because their charged sulphonate/ammonium ends do not precipitate with Ca2+ or Mg2+ ions.
